title: The violin as lead instrument in New Orleans bands
summary: Johnny was a professional violinist and trombonist; the violin led the seven-piece band and Emil Bigard was a good reader who taught tunes by ear.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Fiddlers and reading violinists of New Orleans

blocks.x: 30. Tootie, was Johnnie a professional musician?
Yeah. He was a professional. Yeah. He played the violin.
I see. Now, a lot of people wonder what the violin did in New Orleans music. Maybe you could tell us a little bit about that.
Well, the violin, you know, you take the violin -- we had a seven piece band, you know. He played all the leads, you know.
That's the lead instrument, you know.
And no piano. You had your guitar.
Your bass. Drum, clarinet, trombone, and trumpet.
And the violin played the leads.
The violin played the lead, you know. He'd always knock off the pieces, you know.
Uh-huh. Right. Did the violin player often read music, too?
Yeah. We had a group, we had a violin player name of Bigard. That's Barney's uncle.
Well, Emil would play the pieces, get his violin and play all them tunes, you know, start off and give us the cue on how to play them, you know.
Oh, you wouldn't know. Wasn't nobody could read nothing.
He played. Just that quick. Said, 'Let's go,' and he started to playing it, and the band would just play it.
Now, when the -- so, then, the violinist often read very well, and he would be the leader, sometimes, of the bands?
